title: Theoretical Foundations and Effective Algorithms for Policy-Aware Simulator Learning

paper.title: Theoretical Foundations and Effective Algorithms for Policy-Aware Simulator Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) agents typically learn world
models by minimizing predictive loss. However, powerful RL optimizers
inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies, leading to “simulator
exploitation” and a reality gap where policies succeed in simulation
but fail in the real world. We propose that the objective for learning simulators should be strategic robustness rather than predictive accuracy, and
formulate this as a zero-sum minimax game between a model player and
an adversarial policy player. We provide a comprehensive theoretical
analysis: (1) an online learning guarantee showing the game is
learnable with sublinear regret bounds; (2) a tractable critic-based
simplification bounding the global policy-value gap by the local
critic’s loss; and (3) an Error-MDP duality , proving that
finding the worst-case policy is formally dual to a standard RL
problem where the reward is the one-step critic error. This duality
yields a provably convergent active data selection algorithm.
Experiments on continuous control tasks demonstrate that our approach
reduces prediction error in strategically important regions by 1.5 1.5 – 2.2 × 2.2\times and enables policies trained purely in simulation
to match near-optimal real-world performance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) represents a promising path toward agents with high sample efficiency, strong planning capabilities, and the ability to test policies in a safe, offline environment ( Sutton, 1990 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ) . In this paradigm, an agent first learns a simulator, or “world model” ( M ^ \widehat{M} ), from data collected in the real world ( M M ). Second, the agent trains its policy ( π \pi ) entirely within this learned simulator, using it as a fast and safe sandbox to find an optimal strategy. The critical flaw in this decoupled approach is the inevitable discrepancy between the learned model and the true environment. No matter how much data is collected or how large the model, the simulator is never a perfect copy of reality. This discrepancy leads to a well-known failure mode: the reinforcement learning algorithm, as a powerful optimizer, will inevitably discover and exploit the tiniest inaccuracies in the simulator’s physics or rules to achieve an artificially high score ( Chua et al., 2018 ) . This phenomenon, often called the reality gap or simulator exploitation , results in policies that are brilliant in simulation but fail catastrophically when deployed in the real world. The standard approach to simulator learning is to minimize a one-step predictive loss, such as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) or the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). This objective, however, is fundamentally misaligned with the agent’s downstream task. MLE optimizes for average predictive accuracy across all visited states, whereas the RL agent’s performance is determined by the worst-case, exploitable error along the specific trajectories it discovers. A model can have 99% predictive accuracy on average but fail on a single, crucial transition that an adversary can learn to visit repeatedly. Existing work has proposed several ways to mitigate this. One popular method is to learn an ensemble of models to quantify uncertainty ( Chua et al., 2018 ) and train a policy that is robust to this distribution. Another line of work, particularly in offline RL, introduces pessimism or conservatism, penalizing the agent for actions that deviate from the known data ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . A third category uses robust control formulations, but these often require a pre-defined and known ”uncertainty set” for the dynamics ( Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ; Wiesemann et al., 2013 ) , which is unavailable when the model is learned. More recently, adversarial methods have been explored. Some works introduce adversarial disturbances to the state ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) rather than the model itself. Others use Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to train the simulator, using a critic to enforce that one-step transitions are ”realistic” ( Volodin et al., 2023 ) . While promising, this still optimizes a local, one-step metric of realism. It fails to address the global, policy-level objective of strategic robustness . The critic does not ask, Is this transition plausible? ; it should ask, Can a policy exploit this transition to create an unrealistic, high-value trajectory? To bridge this gap from local plausibility to global strategic robustness, we argue for a new objective. We reframe simulator learning not as a prediction task, but as a two-player, zero-sum game between a Model Player (the simulator) and a Policy Player (the adversary). The Policy Player’s goal is to find the policy π \pi that reveals the largest discrepancy between the true value in the real world V π ​ ( M ) V_{\pi}(M) and the predicted value in the simulator V π ​ ( M ^ ) V_{\pi}(\widehat{M}) . The Model Player’s goal is to update its parameters to minimize this worst-case discrepancy. This leads to our central minimax objective: min M ^ ∈ ℳ ⁡ max π ∈ Π ​ | V π ​ ( M ) − V π ​ ( M ^ ) | \displaystyle\min_{\widehat{M}\in\mathcal{M}}\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\,\left\lvert V_{\pi}(M)-V_{\pi}(\widehat{M})\right\rvert (1) By solving this game, we produce a simulator that is not just accurate on average, but is specifically robust against being exploited by the very agent that will be trained within it. This formulation also provides a principled theoretical foundation for related proxy hacking problems, such as reward hacking in RLHF ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Christiano et al., 2017 ) and out-of-distribution exploitation in offline RL ( Levine et al., 2020 ) . Our contributions are as follows: • A Policy-Aware Minimax Objective: We formulate robust simulator learning as a minimax game and connect it to a practical online learning framework. We provide a regret bound (Theorem 3 ) showing that if the model player achieves sublinear regret, its average value-gap against the adversary also vanishes. • Tractable Critic-Based Guarantees: We show that the intractable policy-maximization max π \max_{\pi} in ( 1 ) can be relaxed to a tractable max D \max_{D} over a critic function D D . We provide finite-time guarantees (Lemma 4 ) that bound the true policy-value gap by the loss of this critic-based game, scaled by a coverage constant κ \kappa . • The Error-MDP Duality: We introduce our most significant theoretical novelty. We prove (Theorem 9 ) that the global problem of finding the worst-case policy π \pi is formally dual to a local RL problem: finding the optimal policy in an Error-MDP where the reward is precisely the one-step critic error. • Provably Stable Active Learning: We resolve the circular dependency between learning a model and collecting its counter-examples. We formalize active data selection as an iterative game and prove its convergence to a saddle point (Theorem 11 ). This guarantees that our critic-guided sampling mechanism is not merely heuristic, but a theoretically stable method for minimizing the coverage constant κ \kappa . • A General Framework for Proxy Hacking: We show this framework is a general solution for proxy hacking , with direct applications to solving reward hacking in RLHF and OOD-exploitation in Offline RL (Section 8 ).

sections.heading: Related Work.
sections.text: Our approach intersects with several key areas. Uncertainty-aware MBRL relies on ensembles or pessimism to mitigate model error, whereas we actively seek and correct strategic flaws. Adversarial RL typically perturbs dynamics to robustify policies; in contrast, we perturb policies to robustify models. Finally, Value-Aware Model Learning weights errors by value gradients for a fixed policy, while our minimax formulation actively anticipates the worst-case policy shift. We provide an extended discussion in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Paper Organization.
sections.text: The paper is organized as follows. Section 3 formalizes the landscape of simulator fidelity metrics and justifies our choice. Section 4 presents our first main result, an online-learning guarantee for the full minimax objective. Section 5 introduces our practical, critic-based simplification of the game and provides robust value-gap guarantees. Section 6 presents our novel theoretical results on active data selection, including the Error-MDP duality and convergence proofs. In Section 7 , we present an experimental validation of our theoretical results by examining a controlled 2D scenario. Section 8 discusses the broader applications of our framework to other proxy-hacking problems. Section 9 generalizes our framework to the joint learning of dynamics and rewards.

sections.heading:
3 What Should a Good Simulator Match?
Metrics and Desiderata
sections.text: Before formalizing our minimax objective, we must first establish what it means for a simulator to be good . In standard supervised learning, fidelity is measured by predictive accuracy on a fixed dataset. In reinforcement learning, however, fidelity is measured by the success of policies trained within the simulator when deployed in the real world. This distinction requires a careful choice of metric. For clarity, throughout the main analysis we identify the true world model M M with its transition kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} , and the simulator M ^ \widehat{M} with 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} , treating the reward function r r as known. We denote by P 𝖯 π P_{\mathsf{P}}^{\pi} the marginal distribution over finite trajectory prefixes (e.g. length- H H segments). The discounted state-action occupancy for π \pi under 𝖯 \mathsf{P} is d π 𝖯 ( s , a ) = 𝔼 [ ∑ t = 0 ∞ γ t 𝟏 { ( s t , a t ) = ( s , a ) } ] , d_{\pi}^{\mathsf{P}}(s,a)=\E\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathbf{1}\{(s_{t},a_{t})=(s,a)\}\right], and the one-step conditional transition at ( s , a ) (s,a) is 𝖯 ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) \mathsf{P}(\cdot\mid s,a) . Below we consider several notions of simulator fidelity, ranging from the strongest (trajectory-level) to the weakest (optimal-value only).

sections.heading: 3.1 Trajectory or reward-free closeness
sections.text: Definition 1 . We say 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} is trajectory-close to 𝖯 \mathsf{P} (for horizon H H ) if some divergence between their finite-horizon trajectory distributions is small: D traj ( H ) ( 𝖯 , 𝖯 ^ ) = sup π ∈ Π D ( P 𝖯 π ( τ 0 : H − 1 ) , P 𝖯 ^ π ( τ 0 : H − 1 ) ) , D_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(H)}(\mathsf{P},\widehat{\mathsf{P}})=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}D\left(P_{\mathsf{P}}^{\pi}(\tau_{0:H-1}),P_{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}^{\pi}(\tau_{0:H-1})\right), where D D is a divergence such as TV, KL, or Wasserstein. This is a reward-free criterion: if trajectory distributions match, then all reward functions measurable on trajectories, including state- or action-dependent ones, induce the same return distributions. It is extremely strong: matching trajectory distributions implies matching all marginals, including ( s , a ) (s,a) occupancies and one-step conditionals, but is infeasible for large or continuous state spaces. For discounted infinite-horizon problems one can instead consider the distribution over discounted trajectories. In practice, one truncates to large H H and weights by γ t \gamma^{t} . This metric corresponds to the ideal of a “Digital Twin”, that is a simulator that captures the physics of the environment so indistinguishably that an outside observer cannot tell the difference. While desirable, we argue that when the model class is misspecified (limited capacity), striving for this physical perfection is inefficient compared to optimizing for strategic equivalence.

sections.heading: 3.5 Implications and recommendations
sections.text: The logical relationships between the criteria are straightforward: trajectory closeness (Subsection 3.1 ) implies one-step matching (Subsection 3.2 ), which in turn implies policy-value matching (Subsection 3.3 ), as follows from standard simulation lemmas. The converse directions generally fail unless the dynamics satisfy additional structural constraints. Furthermore, equality of values for all deterministic stationary policies already guarantees equality for all stationary randomized policies, owing to linearity in state-action occupancies. By contrast, requiring only that optimal values coincide, as in (Subsection 3.4 ), is far too weak to ensure the successful transfer of policies across environments. From both a theoretical and a practical perspective, the most promising compromise seems to be to train simulators using occupancy-weighted, value-aware one-step losses . Specifically, we can seek to minimize min 𝖯 ^ 𝔼 ( s , a ) ∼ μ [ D one-step ( 𝖯 ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) , 𝖯 ^ ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) ) ] , \min_{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}\E_{(s,a)\sim\mu}\left[D_{\text{one-step}}(\mathsf{P}(\cdot\mid s,a),\widehat{\mathsf{P}}(\cdot\mid s,a))\right], where μ \mu is an occupancy measure concentrating on the regions of the state–action space visited by policies of interest. In the theoretical analysis of Section 4 , choosing D one-step = 𝖣 KL D_{\text{one-step}}=\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}} yields the occupancy-weighted KL divergence 𝔼 d π [ 𝖣 KL ( 𝖯 ∥ 𝖯 ^ ) ] \E_{d_{\pi}}[\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf{P}\|\widehat{\mathsf{P}})] , which not only provides an upper bound on the policy value gap but also admits an interpretation as a regret-like objective in an online-learning framework. In continuous or high-dimensional state spaces, it is often preferable to replace the KL divergence with weaker, geometry-aware distances such as the Wasserstein or Sinkhorn metrics. These respect the underlying geometry of the state space, are more robust to estimation noise, and can be combined with KL-based analysis to obtain hybrid surrogates that balance tractability and fidelity. In practice, model learning should focus on the reachable region of the state space, that is, the subset of states visited by near-optimal or adversarial policies. Matching trajectories globally is typically infeasible and unnecessary; fidelity within this region is what ultimately determines policy robustness and transfer performance. Finally, of course, empirical evaluations could report several complementary metrics, including the occupancy-weighted one-step KL or TV divergence, short-horizon trajectory Wasserstein distance, and the worst-case value-gap over a held-out policy set. Each captures different aspects of simulator fidelity and exposes distinct failure modes. Overall, the most useful and theoretically grounded criterion for decision-making seems to be an occupancy-weighted, value-aware one-step divergence, typically the expected KL divergence under relevant occupancies, or a Wasserstein analogue for continuous spaces. This criterion is weaker, and therefore more practical, than full trajectory matching, yet substantially stronger and more decision-relevant than aligning only the optimal values. With these metrics in hand, we now formalize the minimax game that optimizes for strategic robustness. Example: case of minimal MDPs. Consider a true environment 𝖬 \mathsf{M} with high-entropy, irrelevant noise (e.g., a TV playing static in the background) and its minimal equivalent 𝖬 ′ \mathsf{M}^{\prime} (a bisimulation that ignores the static). Under a reward-free metric like trajectory KL (Subsection 3.1 ), 𝖬 ′ \mathsf{M}^{\prime} is a poor simulator because it fails to model the complex noise of 𝖬 \mathsf{M} . But, under our strategic objective (Subsection 3.3 ), 𝖬 ′ \mathsf{M}^{\prime} is a perfect simulator, as V π ​ ( 𝖬 ) = V π ​ ( 𝖬 ′ ) V_{\pi}(\mathsf{M})=V_{\pi}(\mathsf{M}^{\prime}) for all π \pi . This illustrates why predictive accuracy (modeling the noise) is often misaligned with robust control. Our framework favors 𝖬 ′ \mathsf{M}^{\prime} , dedicating capacity only to dynamics that affect the value function. A concrete example is a Block MDP, where the control problem can be solved entirely in the latent space. A reward-free metric might waste capacity modeling the complex, high-dimensional mapping from latents to observations, whereas our strategic objective focuses solely on the latent dynamics required to estimate value.

sections.heading: 5 Game Formulation using Upper-Bounds
sections.text: Since learning a simulator by maximum likelihood estimation is standard, it may appear natural to approximate the objective in ( 1 ) using negative log likelihood losses. This indeed yields a valid approach which we discussed and analyzed in the previous section. While this gives strong guarantees (see Theorem 3 ), it involves a maximization over the entire policy space, which can be computationally expensive. Moreover, evaluating the negative log likelihood loss requires knowledge of the true dynamics 𝖯 \mathsf{P} to compute the KL divergence. We here instead present a tractable simplification. We replace the intractable max π \max_{\pi} player with a feasible max D \max_{D} player, a critic, and substitute the KL loss with a dual-divergence loss that can be estimated directly from samples. However, this projection may sacrifice accuracy in strategic regions to fit irrelevant stochasticity elsewhere, as discussed in the Minimal MDP example. Since ℳ \mathscr{M} is deterministic, 𝖯 ^ MLE \widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{\text{MLE}} might oscillate or predict the mean of the noise, potentially distorting the relevant dynamics to minimize the global KL/MSE, leading to high strategic error. • 𝖯 ^ MM \widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{\text{MM}} minimizes the worst-case value gap. sections.heading: 6 Active Data Selection for Improved Coverage Guarantees
sections.text: The coverage-based guarantees in Theorem 5 and 6 are powerful, but they depend critically on the coverage constant κ \kappa of the data distribution d data d_{\mathrm{data}} relative to the policies of interest Π \Pi . This raises a chicken-and-egg problem: to get a good guarantee, one must sample from a distribution d data d_{\mathrm{data}} that already covers the occupancies d π d_{\pi} of the very policies π \pi that might exploit the simulator. This suggests an active learning approach, where the sampling distribution d t d_{t} is updated iteratively to find these exploitative policies. We now present our most significant theoretical insight. We show that the global problem of finding the worst-case policy π \pi is formally equivalent to a local reinforcement learning problem: finding the optimal policy in an Error-MDP where the reward signal is precisely the one-step modeling error. We first define a new Error-MDP , 𝖬 err \mathsf{M}_{\text{err}} , which has the same state space 𝒮 \mathscr{S} , action space 𝒜 \mathscr{A} , and true transition dynamics 𝖯 \mathsf{P} as the real environment, but with a different reward function. The concept of using model error as an intrinsic reward has been explored empirically in active exploration methods like MCX ( Gehring et al., 2024 ) ; here, we provide the formal duality proving that this strategy is not just a heuristic, but the optimal response in a minimax robustness game. Define the error-reward r err r_{\text{err}} as the local, one-step modeling error, as measured by our Wasserstein-based critic r err ​ ( s , a ) = W 1 ​ ( 𝖯 ⁡ ( s , a ) , 𝖯 ^ ​ ( s , a ) ) r_{\text{err}}(s,a)=W_{1}\big(\mathsf{P}(s,a),\widehat{\mathsf{P}}(s,a)\big) . The following theorem proves that the worst-case policy value-gap (our original objective) is directly upper-bounded by the optimal value of this Error-MDP. 9 Adversarial Policy as Error-Seeking Agent. Assume V π 𝖯 ^ V_{\pi}^{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}} is L v L_{v} -Lipschitz for all π ∈ Π \pi\in\Pi . The theorem implies that for any policy π \pi , the performance gap between the true MDP and the simulator is upper-bounded (up to a constant) by the value of the corresponding Error-MDP. Consequently, a policy that achieves a large Error-MDP value is likely to also induce a large discrepancy in returns. This observation motivates treating the Error-MDP as a proxy optimization problem for identifying policies that expose weaknesses in the learned model, a standard RL problem we can solve using familiar algorithms. The Error-MDP provides a principled mechanism to identify where the learned model 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} is inaccurate. Its optimal policy naturally seeks trajectories that accumulate large modeling errors, thereby revealing parts of the state–action space that lack sufficient coverage. Using this policy for active sampling directs exploration toward these high-error regions, improving model accuracy and coverage, and thus tightening the worst-case performance bound guaranteed by the theorem. Note that our Error-MDP framework provides a theoretical justification for intrinsic motivation ( Chentanez et al., 2005 ) . While methods like random network distillation (RND) ( Burda et al., 2019 ) use prediction error as a heuristic for novelty, our Theorem 9 proves that maximizing model error is the optimal adversarial strategy for robust simulator learning. This also suggests that off-the-shelf exploration algorithms (like PPO with intrinsic rewards) can be directly plugged in as the Policy Player in our game.

sections.heading: 7 Experimental Validation of Theory
sections.text: We empirically validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the practicality of our approach in a series of experiments. First, we illustrate Algorithm 3 on a narrow passage domain, showing that the critic accurately identifies model deficiencies (validating Theorems 9 and 11 ). Second, we compare simulation accuracy on five high-dimensional benchmarks with generative sampling access, testing the predictions of Theorem 3 regarding strategic error reduction. Third, we demonstrate the downstream benefits in one of the hardest use cases for simulators: training a policy purely in simulation without any further regularization such as pessimism. Finally, we empirically validate the convergence stability of the minimax game (Section 7.4 ).

sections.heading: 7.1 Illustration on Narrow Passage domain
sections.text: We use a simple version of a narrow passage navigation domain for illustration. The agent can move in a 2d plane, starts on the left and has to reach the right of the state space. The space is divided in half by a vertical wall with only a small gap in the middle. In front and inside this narrow passage, there is a strong wind pushing the agent downward. See Figure 2 (c, left) for an illustration. Simulator training starts with data collected by a random policy and uniformly sampled initial states. This fails to appropriately cover the narrow passage region where the winds are not predicted accurately. Figure 2 (a) shows that the critic D D accurately captures this. Thus, the next iterations of Algorithm 3 focus on this region (Figure 2 (b)), which reduces the simulator error in the narrow passage so that the final model accurately captures the complex wind dynamics (Figure 2 (c)).

sections.heading: 7.2 Evaluation of Simulation Accuracy on High-Dimensional Control Tasks
sections.text: We now validate Algorithm 3 on a suite of high-dimensional continuous-control environments with generative sampling access. These experiments test whether the minimax formulation delivers tangible improvements in simulation accuracy when the training data distribution is biased away from high-sensitivity regions, the precise setting in which Theorem 3 predicts the largest gains.

sections.heading: Setup and Evaluation.
sections.text: We consider five environments with state dimensionality ranging from 3 3 to 23 23 , each incorporating non-trivial transition dynamics with distinct high-sensitivity regions : discontinuities (ground contact, joint limits), nonlinear damping, and sharp turbulence thresholds. Training data is generated by sampling transitions from state-action pairs with a distribution bias that under-represents high-sensitivity regions, simulating the setting where a behavioral policy avoids challenging states. The test set is drawn uniformly across the full state-action space. This creates a genuine distribution mismatch: the training data concentrates on benign regions, while the test evaluation includes all of the high-sensitivity transitions that matter for downstream policy performance. We compare Algorithm 3 with active sampling against a standard maximum-likelihood estimator trained on the biased initial data (minimizing ℓ 2 \ell_{2} loss uniformly over the training samples). sections.heading:
7.3 Evaluation of Stand-alone Policy Training in Simulation on Control
Tasks
sections.text: Having demonstrated that Algorithm 3 leads to tangible improvements in simulation accuracy, we now evaluate how such improvements translate to better policy performance in one of the hardest applications of a simulator: training a policy purely in simulation to perform well in the real world. This setting is a much more difficult compared to those typically tackled by model-based RL works, as there is no access to the real world domain whatsoever during training of the final policy for evaluation. We demonstrate this on several control tasks from the Deepmind Control Suite ( Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020 ) and Gymnasium ( Towers et al., 2024 ) . Algorithm implementation. To implement Algorithm 3 with scalable neural networks, we replace the explicit critic guided distribution in line 6 with a policy gradient update step and use this policy in line 3 to sample transitions for the next iteration. Our implementation builds on SAC for this policy optimization step. Thus, the algorithm maintains 3 neural networks, the critic model D t D_{t} , the simulator model and the data collection policy π t \pi_{t} . Each model is a fully connected neural network with 3 hidden layers of 256 units each and linear activations in the final layer. The critic model outputs the score, the simulator model the reward as well as the mean and log-variance for each dimension of the next state, which is then sampled using a Gaussian distribution. The policy also uses this Gaussian distribution as output. For all details of our implementation, see Appendix F . Baseline. Aside from demonstrating the practicality of Algorithm 3 , our experiments seek to show the benefits of using the iterative Wasserstein critic to guide data collection. We therefore compare Algorithm 3 against a baseline which collects data using the SAC algorithm and learns the simulator model using maximum likelihood estimation – cross entropy loss for state transitions and mean squared error for reward prediction. Each method uses the same architectures for policy and simulator. Setup and Evaluation. We run each method for 1M steps in the real environment, the Mujoco task and afterwards evaluate the final learned simulator. For evaluation, we train a new policy using the SAC algorithm with only access to the simulator and measure the reward this policy achieves in the real environment. Results. Figure 3 shows results on the cart-pole balancing, cart-pole swing-up, pendulum, and reacher tasks. Training using the simulator learned by Algorithm 3 yields stable performance, with the policy reaching close to optimal real-world return within 1M steps in all four tasks. This is in stark contrast to the baseline’s simulator, where the learned policy fails to achieve meaningful performance in 3 out of 4 tasks (cart-pole swing-up, pendulum, and reacher). This demonstrates that data collection driven by strategic robustness yields simulators with a substantially smaller sim-to-real gap, compared to data collection driven entirely by reward maximization, even when both simulators are subsequently used in the exact same reward-maximization policy training. Algorithm 3 achieves close to optimal real-world performance in all four tasks, while the baseline suffers from a severe sim-to-real gap in 3 out of 4 tasks. Results are averaged over 5 independent runs (simulator learning and subsequent policy learning in simulator).

sections.heading: 7.4 Convergence Stability
sections.text: A common concern with minimax objectives is training instability arising from the adversarial game between the model and the critic ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) . In standard GAN training, this instability can manifest in three ways: (i) training divergence, (ii) mode collapse, and (iii) cycling or oscillation around the equilibrium. We address this concern at three levels: a formal convergence guarantee, structural differences from standard GANs, and empirical validation.

sections.heading: Theoretical guarantee.
sections.text: Theorem 11 proves that when both players follow no-regret algorithms, the time-averaged strategies converge to an approximate saddle point at rate O ⁡ ( ( Regret M ⁡ ( T ) + Regret D ⁡ ( T ) ) / T ) O((\Regret_{M}(T)+\Regret_{D}(T))/T) . This directly rules out cycling (iii): the averaged iterates cannot oscillate, since the duality gap is provably decreasing. The KL regularization term λ 𝖣 KL ( d ∥ u ) \lambda\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(d\parallel u) in the payoff ensures the game has a unique saddle point, ruling out the multiplicity of equilibria that causes instability in unregularized minimax problems.

sections.heading: Structural differences from standard GANs.
sections.text: Mescheder et al. (2018) showed that Wasserstein-GANs with gradient penalty do not provably converge locally under standard simultaneous gradient descent. However, our setting differs from standard GANs in several important ways that avoid the specific failure modes identified in their analysis: • Convex-concave structure. Our regularized payoff L ( 𝖯 ^ , d ) = 𝔼 d [ W 1 ( 𝖯 , 𝖯 ^ ) ] − λ 𝖣 KL ( d ∥ u ) L(\widehat{\mathsf{P}},d)=\E_{d}[W_{1}(\mathsf{P},\widehat{\mathsf{P}})]-\lambda\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(d\parallel u) is convex in 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} (as an expectation of the convex Wasserstein distance) and concave in d d (linear minus convex KL). In standard GANs, both players’ losses are non-convex in parameter space, which is the root cause of the cycling dynamics and purely imaginary eigenvalues in the Dirac-GAN analysis. Our convex-concave structure guarantees that the minimax theorem applies and a saddle point exists. • Iterative, non-simultaneous updates. We use an iterative, active-learning RL loop where the data distribution is dynamically updated at each round, rather than a static, simultaneous gradient descent loop. Each round collects new real-world data, retrains the critic, and updates the model sequentially. This avoids the simultaneous-update instabilities analyzed by Mescheder et al. (2018) . • Stochastic model. In our continuous control implementation, the model outputs a stochastic Gaussian distribution (predicting mean and log-variance) rather than a Dirac delta. This provides a smooth loss landscape and avoids the degenerate dynamics of the Dirac-GAN setting. We note that the gradient penalty in our implementation serves a different purpose than in standard WGAN-GP: it is not a training stabilizer per se, but a strict requirement of the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality to enforce the 1-Lipschitz constraint on the critic. This constraint is necessary for the critic to estimate the 1-Wasserstein distance, which is the foundation of our coverage guarantee (Lemma 4 ) and the Error-MDP duality (Theorem 9 ).

sections.heading: Empirical validation.
sections.text: We validate the above analysis empirically by comparing three training regimes on the Hopper (14D) environment: 1. Minimax (stabilized): Algorithm 3 with stabilized importance weights ( w max = 3 w_{\max}=3 ). 2. Minimax (aggressive): Same active sampling but with aggressive, unclipped importance weights ( w max = 10 w_{\max}=10 ). In our implementation, the Lipschitz constraint from Theorem 11 manifests as importance weight clipping, which enforces a bound on how much the effective training distribution can deviate from the base distribution. The stabilized variant clips active sample weights to w max = 3 w_{\max}=3 , while the aggressive variant uses w max = 10 w_{\max}=10 with no clipping safeguard. 3. MLE: Baseline maximum-likelihood training. Figure 4 : Convergence stability analysis on Hopper (14D). (a) Training loss: all three methods converge smoothly, with the minimax variants reaching lower final loss. The MLE curve flattens earlier because it fits only the biased initial data, while the minimax methods continuously incorporate harder active samples, temporarily increasing loss before reducing it again. (b) Critic error across active sampling rounds: the stabilized variant converges with lower variance. (c, d) Final strategic RMSE: Minimax (stabilized) achieves the lowest error ( 0.077 ± 0.006 0.077\pm 0.006 ) with substantially lower inter-seed variance than both the aggressive minimax ( 0.119 ± 0.016 0.119\pm 0.016 ) and MLE ( 0.140 ± 0.006 0.140\pm 0.006 ). The tight confidence interval demonstrates the stabilizing effect of importance weight clipping, which approximates the Lipschitz constraint from Theorem 11 . Figure 4 shows the results across 5 random seeds. The stabilized variant dominates on every metric, addressing each of the three failure modes: (i) all training curves converge smoothly without divergence (Figure 4 a); (ii) the stabilized model achieves the lowest error across all strategic regions, ruling out mode collapse (Figure 4 c,d); and (iii) its inter-seed variance on strategic error is 3 × 3\times smaller than the aggressive version (std. 0.006 0.006 vs. 0.016 0.016 ), confirming that the Lipschitz constraint prevents the oscillatory dynamics predicted by Theorem 11 . The convergence stability analysis (Figure 4 ) further confirms that the minimax training is practical and reliable.

sections.heading: 8 Applications
sections.text: This paper’s core contribution, a minimax framework for learning a robust model, is a general-purpose solution to a critical problem that appears across many domains of reinforcement learning and AI. Our core objective: min M ^ ∈ ℳ ⁡ max π ∈ Π ​ | V π ​ ( M ) − V π ​ ( M ^ ) | \min_{\widehat{M}\in\mathcal{M}}\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\,\left\lvert V_{\pi}(M)-V_{\pi}(\widehat{M})\right\rvert can be generalized to: min Proxy ​ θ ^ ⁡ max Agent ​ π ​ | TrueValue π ​ ( R true ) − ProxyValue π ​ ( R ^ θ ) | \min_{\text{Proxy }\widehat{\theta}}\max_{\text{Agent }\pi}\,\left\lvert\text{TrueValue}_{\pi}(R_{\text{true}})-\text{ProxyValue}_{\pi}(\widehat{R}_{\theta})\right\rvert This Robust Proxy Learning framework applies anywhere an agent optimizes an imperfect, learned model of reality. Here are the two most direct applications.

sections.heading: 8.1 Reward learning and RLHF
sections.text: Our framework directly provides the theoretical foundation for tackling ”reward hacking” in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) . Our solution has some relationship with that of Gupta et al. (2025) , which is also based on a minimax problem. In RLHF, there is no true reward function R R . Instead, a proxy ”reward model” R ^ \widehat{R} is learned from human preference data. Next, a policy π \pi is trained to maximize this proxy: π ∗ = argmax π V π ​ ( R ^ ) \pi^{*}=\argmax_{\pi}V_{\pi}(\widehat{R}) . The problem, ”reward hacking”, is that π ∗ \pi^{*} will inevitably find and exploit inaccuracies in R ^ \widehat{R} to achieve a high score, leading to behavior that is absurd or dangerous according to the true human intent R R . This mirrors recent formalizations of reward hacking as the divergence between a proxy and the true objective ( Laidlaw et al., 2024 ) . This is a perfect analogy to the method described in this work with the following substitutions: True World M M → \to True Reward R R (the human’s intent); Simulator M ^ \widehat{M} → \to Reward Model R ^ \widehat{R} (the learned proxy); Reality Gap → \to Reward Hacking. By substituting terms, our minimax objective becomes the principled objective for RLHF: min R ^ ∈ ℛ ⁡ max π ∈ Π ​ | V π ​ ( R ) − V π ​ ( R ^ ) | . \min_{\widehat{R}\in\mathcal{R}}\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\,\left\lvert V_{\pi}(R)-V_{\pi}(\widehat{R})\right\rvert. This objective reads: Find a reward model R ^ \widehat{R} that is robust to exploitation by the optimal policy π \pi that will be trained on it. Our theoretical contributions map directly: • Active Data Selection (Section 6 ): Our “Error-MDP Duality” theorem (Theorem 9 ) provides the formal justification for active preference learning . – In our context, the ”error reward” is r err = W 1 ​ ( 𝖯 , 𝖯 ^ ) r_{\text{err}}=W_{1}(\mathsf{P},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}) . – In RLHF, the ”error reward” r err = | R ⁡ ( s , a ) − R ^ ​ ( s , a ) | r_{\text{err}}=\lvert R(s,a)-\widehat{R}(s,a)\rvert is unknown; instead we need human feedback. • Our Iterative Algorithm (Algorithm 3 ) becomes the core RLHF loop: 1. Model Player: Train the current reward model R ^ t \widehat{R}_{t} on all human data collected so far. 2. Policy Player (Adversary): Train a policy π t = argmax π V π ​ ( R ^ t ) \pi_{t}=\argmax_{\pi}V_{\pi}(\widehat{R}_{t}) . This policy is the ”adversary” that finds the biggest exploit. 3. Find Error (critic): Present trajectories from π t \pi_{t} to a human. The human provides a correction (for example, ”This is bad behavior, this other trajectory is better”). This human feedback is an empirical sample of the ”error reward” r err r_{\text{err}} . 4. Update Data: Add this new preference data to the dataset. 5. Repeat from step 1. Thus, our framework is not just related to RLHF, it is arguably the formal objective function that the entire iterative RLHF process is seeking to solve.

sections.heading: 8.2 Offline reinforcement learning
sections.text: Our framework also offers a novel perspective on pessimism and conservatism in Offline RL ( Levine et al., 2020 ) . While often framed as a distributional shift problem, offline RL can be rigorously viewed as a proxy-hacking game: the agent attempts to maximize a value function derived from limited data (the proxy), and without constraints, it naturally drifts toward OOD regions where the proxy erroneously predicts high reward. In Offline RL, we learn from a fixed dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . The agent cannot explore. Standard Q-learning fails because the Bellman operator T ⁡ ( Q ) = r + γ ​ max a ′ ⁡ Q ⁡ ( s ′ , a ′ ) T(Q)=r+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}}Q(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}) will exploit any overestimation of Q-values for (state, action) pairs that are out-of-distribution (OOD). The policy ”hacks” the Q-function by steering into regions with no data, where the Q-function is erroneously high. This is again a proxy-hacking problem. We have the following substitutions: True World 𝖬 \mathsf{M} → \to True Bellman Operator T ∗ T^{*} (The operator using the real Q ∗ Q^{*} ); Simulator 𝖬 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{M}} → \to Empirical Bellman Operator T ^ \widehat{T} (The operator using the learned Q Q on data 𝒟 \mathcal{D} ); Reality Gap → \to OOD Exploitation. Conservative and pessimistic Offline RL algorithms (like CQL, MOPO, MOReL) are all heuristics to solve a version of this. They work by penalizing the policy for deviating from the dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Our framework suggests a more direct, two-part approach: 1. Learn a robust simulator from offline data: Instead of learning a Q-function, first learn a simulator M ^ \widehat{M} from the offline dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , using our Theorem 5 (Minimax TV-Critic). This approach aligns with recent adversarial frameworks for offline RL, such as ARMOR ( Bhardwaj et al., 2023 ) , which similarly formulates model learning as a minimax game to optimize a lower bound on performance. • Critic D D : A discriminator trained to distinguish real transitions ( s , a , s ′ ) ∈ 𝒟 (s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D} from simulated transitions ( s , a , s ^ ′ ) ∼ 𝖯 ^ ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) (s,a,\widehat{s}^{\prime})\sim\widehat{\mathsf{P}}(\cdot\mid s,a) . • Model 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} : A generator (our simulator) trained to fool the critic. • This is exactly a GAN trained on the dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Our Theorem 8 provides the guarantee that if the GAN loss J 𝒟 ​ ( 𝖯 ^ ) J_{\mathcal{D}}(\widehat{\mathsf{P}}) is low, the resulting simulator 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} is robust on the data distribution d data d_{\text{data}} . 2. sections.heading: 10 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced a minimax framework for simulator learning that replaces predictive accuracy with strategic robustness as the training objective. By formulating the sim-to-real gap as a zero-sum game, we derived a tractable critic-based bound (Lemma 4 ) that transforms the intractable policy-space maximization into a practical GAN-like training objective. Our central theoretical contribution, the Error-MDP Duality (Theorem 9 ), establishes a formal equivalence between the global problem of finding the worst-case policy and a local RL problem with model error as reward. This duality enables a principled active data selection algorithm whose convergence to a saddle point we proved (Theorem 11 ). Experiments on continuous control benchmarks validate these theoretical predictions: the minimax approach consistently improves simulation accuracy in strategically important regions and enables policies trained purely in simulation to achieve near-optimal real-world performance. Beyond simulator learning, our framework provides a general solution to proxy hacking, applicable to reward hacking in RLHF and out-of-distribution exploitation in offline RL (Section 8 ). Future work could extend the empirical evaluation to generative language models and tackle settings where the sampling distribution cannot be chosen freely. See Appendix C.1 for further discussion.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Discussion of related work
sections.text: Our work addresses the fundamental challenge of learning robust proxy models in reinforcement learning. This intersects with several active research areas. Uncertainty and Pessimism in MBRL. A standard approach to mitigating the reality gap is quantifying epistemic uncertainty, often via model ensembles [ Chua et al., 2018 ] . In Offline RL, where exploration is impossible, this uncertainty is used to penalize the policy, ensuring it stays within the support of the data (pessimism) [ Levine et al., 2020 , Yu et al., 2020 , Kidambi et al., 2020 ] . While effective for avoiding known bad regions, these methods are inherently passive. Our approach is active : it uses the adversary to explicitly find high-uncertainty, exploitable regions and then demands more data from them (via our Error-MDP formulation), rather than just avoiding them. Robust and Adversarial RL. Robust control formulations [ Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 , Wiesemann et al., 2013 ] optimize policies against a worst-case environment chosen from a pre-defined uncertainty set. Our work can be viewed as learning this uncertainty set simultaneously with the policy. Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (ARL) typically introduces an adversary that perturbs dynamics or observations during training [ Pinto et al., 2017 ] . Our framework differs crucially in its target: our adversary does not perturb the state to break the policy; it perturbs the policy to break the model . Adversarial Model Learning. Using GANs to learn environment dynamics is a growing trend. Volodin et al. [2023] propose adversarial world models that use a discriminator to ensure generated transitions are realistic. Our work unifies this with the control objective. A standard GAN discriminator checks if a one-step transition ( s , a , s ′ ) (s,a,s^{\prime}) looks real (local consistency). Our Policy Player checks if an entire sequence of transitions leads to a falsely high value (global strategic consistency). Our theoretical results show that under certain conditions (Wasserstein critics), these local and global objectives can be related, justifying standard GAN-like training as a proxy for our true minimax objective. Dynamics Adaptation and Sim-to-Real. Recent approaches have sought to bridge the gap between source and target dynamics by learning invariant feature representations or adapting policies directly. For instance, Guo et al. [2024] propose DARAIL, which leverages domain adaptation and reward-augmented imitation learning to align the agent’s state distribution with that of an expert in the target domain. However, such methods typically assume the existence of optimal expert demonstrations in the target environment to guide the adaptation. In contrast, our work addresses the unsupervised setting of Simultaneous Policy Learning and Sampling (SPLS), where no target demonstrations are available. Instead of imitating an expert, our Strategic SPLS agent must actively explore the target environment to identify and correct discrepancies in the simulator’s physics, often targeting regions a stable expert would strictly avoid. Value-Aware Model Learning. Prior work has recognized that not all model errors are equal. Value-Aware Model Learning (VAML) [ Farahmand et al., 2017 ] proposes weighting the standard predictive loss by the gradient of the value function, focusing model capacity on states that matter for the current policy. Our work can be viewed as the robust generalization of VAML. Instead of weighting errors based on a single, fixed policy, our minimax framework actively finds the worst-case policy that maximizes these errors, ensuring robustness against future policy shifts. Recent extensions, such as λ \lambda -models [ Voelcker et al., 2023 ] , have similarly recognized the need for iterative updates to resolve the circular dependency between the learned model and the policy’s data distribution. Reward Learning and Alignment. The problem of ”simulator exploitation” in MBRL is formally isomorphic to ”reward hacking” in methods like RLHF [ Christiano et al., 2017 ] . In both cases, an agent optimizes a learned proxy (world model or reward model) and finds adversarial exploits. Recent theoretical work has begun to unify these perspectives [ Gupta et al., 2025 ] . Our Error-MDP duality provides a concrete mechanism, active sampling based on critic disagreement, that is applicable to both domains. Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning. In short, distributionally robust RL [ Shi and Chi, 2024 , e.g.,] aims to find a robust policy given a worst-case simulator in a predefined uncertainty set. Our approach solves the inverse problem: finding a robust simulator that minimizes value prediction error against a worst-case policy. Even without active data collection, the resulting model and policy are distinct in general. There has also been a series of theoretical works which design model-based algorithms with strong regret or PAC learning guarantees [ Sun et al., 2019 , Ayoub et al., 2020 , Foster et al., 2021 , Agarwal and Zhang, 2022 , e.g.,] . While our approach and analysis shares many ideas with this line of work, our focus is slightly different. These works learn a model during policy optimization to improve sample complexity of learning the optimal policy, e.g., in factored MDPs. Instead, our goal is to learn a simulator of the environment, not necessarily tied to optimizing a specific policy but allows us to accurately estimate the value of any policy in the considered set (see the main objective in Equation ( 1 ))

sections.heading: B.2 Lower bounds
sections.text: The rate of convergence derived in Theorem 3 , which scales as O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) , raises a natural question: is this rate fundamental to the problem of learning simulators, or is it an artifact of the analysis? We argue that this rate represents a fundamental limitation of the standard Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) paradigm, stemming from the geometric mismatch between the learning objective and the control objective. Standard model-based RL separates learning into two phases: 1. Estimation: The model 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} minimizes the KL divergence (via MLE) to the true dynamics 𝖯 \mathsf{P} : min 𝖯 ^ 𝔼 d π [ 𝖣 KL ( 𝖯 ∥ 𝖯 ^ ) ] . \min_{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}\E_{d_{\pi}}[\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathsf{P}\parallel\widehat{\mathsf{P}})]. 2. Control: The agent maximizes a value function, whose error scales with the Total Variation (TV) distance (Lemma 12 ): | V π ​ ( 𝖯 ) − V π ​ ( 𝖯 ^ ) | ≤ γ ​ R max 1 − γ ​ 𝔼 d π [ TV ( 𝖯 , 𝖯 ^ ) ] . |V_{\pi}(\mathsf{P})-V_{\pi}(\widehat{\mathsf{P}})|\leq\frac{\gamma R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\E_{d_{\pi}}[\TV(\mathsf{P},\widehat{\mathsf{P}})]. To translate the guarantee from phase 1 (KL) to phase 2 (TV), one must invoke Schützenberger-Pinsker’s inequality [ Rioul, 2023 ] : TV ( P , Q ) ≤ 1 2 𝖣 KL ( P ∥ Q ) \TV(P,Q)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)} . This inequality introduces a square root that degrades the convergence rate. This square-root dependence is optimal near zero [ Rioul, 2023 ] . If a learner achieves a standard fast rate of ϵ ≈ O ( T − 1 / 2 ) \epsilon\approx O(T^{-1/2}) for the KL-divergence (e.g., using parametric MLE), the resulting guarantee for the value gap degrades to: Value Gap ≈ O ( T − 1 / 2 ) = O ( T − 1 / 4 ) \text{Value Gap}\approx\sqrt{O(T^{-1/2})}=O(T^{-1/4}) This Schützenberger-Pinsker tax implies that any method optimizing KL divergence is theoretically inefficient for control, requiring quadratically more samples to achieve the same guarantee on policy performance compared to a method that optimizes the relevant metric directly. This tax is not merely hypothetical; it reflects a divergence in convergence rates for online learning. In the general agnostic setting, standard no-regret algorithms guarantee that the average loss decays at a rate of O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) . • MLE Approach: Minimizes KL. Achieving an average KL error of O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) implies, via Schützenberger-Pinsker’s inequality, a TV error of only O ( T − 1 / 2 ) = O ( T − 1 / 4 ) \sqrt{O(T^{-1/2})}=O(T^{-1/4}) . • Minimax Approach: Minimizes TV directly. By using a loss function that scales linearly with the metric of interest (e.g., Wasserstein or dual-TV), one can theoretically recover the standard O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) rate for the control-relevant error. This O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) vs. O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) gap highlights that MLE-based simulators may be inherently sample-inefficient for control tasks compared to value-aware learners. We provide a formal proposition and rigorous proof of this lower bound in the adversarial setting below. Our proposed Minimax formulation (Section 5 ) circumvents this tax by defining the game directly over the transport metric (TV or Wasserstein) that bounds the value difference. min 𝖯 ^ ⁡ max D ​ 𝔼 ( s , a , s ′ ) ∼ d [ D ⁡ ( s , a , s ′ ) − 𝔼 s ^ ′ ∼ 𝖯 ^ [ D ⁡ ( s , a , s ^ ′ ) ] ] \min_{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}\max_{D}\E_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim d}\left[D(s,a,s^{\prime})-\E_{\widehat{s}^{\prime}\sim\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}[D(s,a,\widehat{s}^{\prime})]\right] Since the loss function is the metric of interest, no conversion inequality is required. Standard results for convex-concave games suggest that such objectives can theoretically achieve the faster O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) rates, verifying that our approach is not just strategically robust, but potentially sample-efficient in a way that MLE cannot be. We argued above that minimizing KL divergence (via MLE) incurs a Schützenberger-Pinsker tax that degrades the convergence rate for control tasks from O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) to O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) . Here, we provide a rigorous justification for this claim. We show that in the adversarial online learning setting, even if the problem is realizable, any learner incurring the standard Ω ⁡ ( T ) \Omega(\sqrt{T}) regret on the negative log-likelihood loss is necessarily limited by Ω ( T − 1 / 4 ) \Omega(T^{-1/4}) average error in the Total Variation distance. Proposition 14 (Lower Bound for Metric-Mismatched Learning) . Consider the online learning of a sequence of probability distributions P 1 , … , P T P_{1},\dots,P_{T} selected by an adversary from a convex class ℳ \mathcal{M} . Assume the realizable setting, where for every step t t , the true distribution P t P_{t} is contained in ℳ \mathcal{M} . Let 𝖯 ^ t \widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t} be the model chosen by the learner at round t t . If the learner suffers the standard adversarial regret lower bound for the KL divergence loss: ∑ t = 1 T 𝖣 KL ( P t ∥ 𝖯 ^ t ) ≥ Ω ( T ) \sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{t}\|\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\geq\Omega(\sqrt{T}) , then the average Total Variation error is lower-bounded by: 1 T ∑ t = 1 T TV ( P t , 𝖯 ^ t ) ≥ Ω ( T − 1 / 4 ) . \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV(P_{t},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\geq\Omega(T^{-1/4}). In the realizable setting, the best fixed model (which is the true sequence itself) has zero KL divergence. Therefore, the cumulative sum of KL divergences is exactly equal to the Regret. Given the assumption of Ω ⁡ ( T ) \Omega(\sqrt{T}) regret: ∑ t = 1 T 𝖣 KL ( P t ∥ 𝖯 ^ t ) ≥ c 1 T \sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{t}\|\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\geq c_{1}\sqrt{T} . Dividing by T T , the average KL error is lower-bounded by: 1 T ∑ t = 1 T 𝖣 KL ( P t ∥ 𝖯 ^ t ) ≥ c 1 T − 1 / 2 . \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{t}\|\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\geq c_{1}T^{-1/2}. (3) For parametric families (and generally locally around the true distribution), the KL divergence behaves quadratically with respect to the statistical distance (TV). Specifically, there exist distributions P , Q P,Q such that 𝖣 KL ( P ∥ Q ) ≤ c 2 TV ( P , Q ) 2 . \mathsf{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\leq c_{2}\TV(P,Q)^{2}. Combining with the regret lower bound from Eq. ( 3 ): c 2 ​ ∑ t = 1 T TV ( P t , 𝖯 ^ t ) 2 ≥ c 1 ​ T . c_{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV(P_{t},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})^{2}\geq c_{1}\sqrt{T}. Dividing by T T and applying Jensen’s inequality ( ( 1 T ​ ∑ x i ) 2 ≤ 1 T ​ ∑ x i 2 \left(\frac{1}{T}\sum x_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum x_{i}^{2} ): ( 1 T ∑ t = 1 T TV ( P t , 𝖯 ^ t ) ) 2 ≤ 1 T ∑ t = 1 T TV ( P t , 𝖯 ^ t ) 2 ⇒ ( 1 T ∑ t = 1 T TV ) 2 ≥ c 1 c 2 T − 1 / 2 . \left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV(P_{t},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\right)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV(P_{t},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})^{2}\Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV\right)^{2}\geq\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}T^{-1/2}. Taking the square root yields: 1 T ∑ t = 1 T TV ( P t , 𝖯 ^ t ) ≥ c 1 c 2 ( T − 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 = Ω ( T − 1 / 4 ) . \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\TV(P_{t},\widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t})\geq\sqrt{\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}}(T^{-1/2})^{1/2}=\Omega(T^{-1/4}). This completes the proof. ∎ It is important to distinguish this result from standard batch (I.I.D.) learning. • I.I.D. Setting: In standard statistical estimation, Maximum Likelihood Estimation is asymptotically efficient and achieves “fast rates” of O ⁡ ( 1 / T ) O(1/T) for the KL divergence. In this specific case, the TV error decays as O ⁡ ( 1 / T ) = O ( T − 1 / 2 ) \sqrt{O(1/T)}=O(T^{-1/2}) . Since direct TV minimization also typically achieves O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) , there is no rate penalty in the batch setting. • Adversarial Setting: However, our work focuses on the Adversarial setting (Section 4 ), where the distribution sequence is chosen adaptively by a Policy Player. In this general online learning setting, fast rates are impossible without strong curvature assumptions, and the minimax regret is lower bounded by Ω ⁡ ( T ) \Omega(\sqrt{T}) . Consequently, in the adversarial setting relevant to robust control, the geometric mismatch between KL and TV incurs a genuine rate penalty ( T − 1 / 4 T^{-1/4} vs T − 1 / 2 T^{-1/2} ), justifying the need for the direct Minimax formulation proposed in this paper. A theoretical counter-argument might suggest that because the KL divergence is strongly convex with respect to the L 1 L_{1} norm (or exp-concave), one could achieve logarithmic regret O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) , corresponding to an average rate of O ⁡ ( 1 / T ) O(1/T) . If this were possible, the TV error would scale as 1 / T = T − 1 / 2 \sqrt{1/T}=T^{-1/2} , recovering the standard rate. However, in the context of learning deep simulators, these fast rates are generally inaccessible for two key reasons: 1. Non-Convex Parameterization: While the negative log-likelihood is convex in the space of probability distributions P P , it is highly non-convex with respect to the parameters θ \theta of a neural network. Standard gradient-based algorithms (like Adam or SGD) used in Deep RL do not satisfy the strong convexity assumptions required for logarithmic regret in parameter space. 2. High Dimensionality: Algorithms that theoretically achieve fast rates for exp-concave losses (such as the Online Newton Step) typically incur computational costs or regret bounds that scale poorly with the dimension d d of the parameter space (e.g., O ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ T ) O(d\log T) regret with O ⁡ ( d 2 ) O(d^{2}) or O ⁡ ( d 3 ) O(d^{3}) runtime). For modern world models where d d is in the millions, these methods are computationally intractable. Consequently, practical Deep Model-Based Reinforcement Learning is constrained to the regime of first-order optimization with O ⁡ ( T ) O(\sqrt{T}) regret. In this regime, the geometric mismatch between KL and TV derived in Proposition 14 incurs a genuine performance penalty compared to direct Minimax optimization.

sections.heading: C.1 Limitations
sections.text: Our approach assumes that active sampling in the real environment is possible during simulator learning. This is true in many real-world applications but there may be cases where the sampling distribution is more constraint or even fixed. Our approach could still be used in such cases, e.g., by dataset reweighting but we did not investigate this. While our algorithmic approach is broadly applicable to various settings and tasks, our empirical evaluation only covers control tasks as they are meaningful benchmarks with sufficient complexity and allow assessing the methodological improvements. However, a more extensive evaluation on other domains such as generative language models could be of interest in future work.

sections.heading: Appendix F Algorithm Implementation and Experimental Details
sections.text: In this section, we detail the practical implementation of our minimax simulator learning framework. We adopt the formulation from Algorithm 3 but introduce two crucial modifications for stability and efficiency: (1) we enforce the Lipschitz constraint on the critic using a gradient penalty as is standard in WGAN-GP (Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty) [ Gulrajani et al., 2017 ] ; and (2) we constrain the adversarial exploration to task-relevant regions.

sections.heading: F.1 Task-aware active sampling via constrained optimization
sections.text: While our theory defines a zero-sum game over the space of all policies Π \Pi , in practice we are primarily interested in the simulator’s accuracy on the manifold of states visited by competent agents. A pure minimax adversary might focus on modeling complex but irrelevant dynamics (e.g., the chaotic motion of a robot after it has already fallen/failed), which wastes sampling budget on regions that do not contribute to task performance. To formally address this, we reframe the sampling step. Instead of an unconstrained maximization of model error, we formulate it as a constrained optimization problem. We seek the policy π \pi that maximizes the estimator’s error (finding the model’s blind spots) subject to the constraint that the policy remains competent at the task, achieving a return above a threshold V min V_{\min} . max π ∈ Π 𝔼 π [ ∑ t = 0 H D ⁡ ( s t , a t , s t + 1 ) ] s.t. sections.heading: F.2 Algorithm details and representation
sections.text: The full procedure is summarized in Algorithm 4 . It proceeds in three key iterative steps: 1. Metric Learning (Critic Step). We update the critic D D to maximize the Wasserstein distance between real transitions ( s , a , s ′ ) (s,a,s^{\prime}) and dreamed transitions ( s , a , s ′′ ) (s,a,s^{\prime\prime}) . • Representation: The critic D ϕ ​ ( s , a , s ′ ) D_{\phi}(s,a,s^{\prime}) is a standard multi-layer perceptron neural network (MLP). Crucially, the final layer is a linear projection without activation (that is, no Sigmoid or Tanh). This is required because the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality defines the distance as a supremum over 1-Lipschitz functions f : 𝒮 → ℝ f\colon\mathscr{S}\to\mathbb{R} , which must be unbounded. Sigmoid activations would restrict the range to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , collapsing the metric to the Jensen-Shannon divergence. • Gradient penalty: To enforce the Lipschitz constraint required for the linear objective to be valid, we apply a gradient penalty λ GP \lambda_{\mathrm{GP}} to the norm of the critic’s gradients. 2. Simulator Learning (Model Step). The model 𝖯 ^ θ \widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{\theta} is updated to fool the critic. • Representation: The model can be represented as a probabilistic neural network (e.g., an ensemble of Gaussian MLPs) that outputs the parameters of a distribution s ′′ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ θ ​ ( s , a ) , Σ θ ​ ( s , a ) ) s^{\prime\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(s,a),\Sigma_{\theta}(s,a)) . Gradients are propagated through the sampling step using the reparameterization trick. • Linear Objective: We update the model via gradient ascent on 𝔼 [ D ⁡ ( s , a , s ′′ ) ] \E[D(s,a,s^{\prime\prime})] . Unlike standard GANs which often require a log-loss surrogate (e.g., log ⁡ D \log D ) to prevent vanishing gradients when the discriminator saturates, our use of the Wasserstein metric with WGAN-GP ensures that the critic provides useful linear gradients even when the model is far from the target. Thus, we optimize the linear objective directly, preserving the theoretical connection to the W 1 W_{1} distance. • While we use the linear objective to guide the data collection, we also train a second model using log-loss on the same data and use this as the final simulator. Depending on the model architecture, this can help improve generalization. Importantly, unlike in GANs, the log-loss surrogate trained model is not affecting the metric learning and data collection. 3. Active Sampling (Policy Step). The policy π ψ \pi_{\psi} is updated to maximize the hybrid reward r sample r_{\mathrm{sample}} derived above. This guides data collection toward regions where the current model 𝖯 ^ t \widehat{\mathsf{P}}_{t} has high discrepancy from the real dynamics, while staying on the manifold of relevant tasks. Sample vs. Computational Efficiency. We acknowledge that Algorithm 3 involves solving an inner RL problem (optimizing π \pi in the Error-MDP) at each iteration. While computationally more intensive than standard MLE or heuristic uncertainty sampling (e.g., ensembles), this cost is justified in settings where real-world samples are the scarce resource (e.g., robotics, medical AI). Our framework effectively trades increased offline computation for minimized real-world interaction, ensuring that every sample collected targets a strategically relevant deficiency in the model. Furthermore, we note that finding the exact optimal policy π ∗ \pi^{*} for the Error-MDP at every iteration is not strictly necessary. In practice, taking a few gradient steps on the policy (e.g., via PPO) to improve its error-seeking capability is sufficient to discover new, high-error regions, making the inner loop computationally tractable. The direct implementation of Algorithm 3 samples from the real environment iteratively, similar to standard MBRL methods. However, in computationally constrained settings, one can decouple this by maintaining a replay buffer and using importance sampling to sample heavily from the buffer’s historical data, falling back on the real environment only when the buffer lacks coverage in the high-error regions identified by the critic. Inaccurate critic predictions harming training? Please note that initial inaccuracies in the critic do not derail training because the algorithm is inherently self-correcting. If the critic falsely assigns a high error score to a specific state-action pair, the sampling distribution will place high probability mass there. In the next iteration, the algorithm will collect ground-truth samples from exactly this pair, automatically correcting both the critic’s estimate and the simulator’s accuracy in that region. sections.heading: F.3 Additional Details on Experimental Setup
sections.text: We build our implementation for the experiments on policy training in control tasks on top of the Acme framework [ Hoffman et al., 2020 ] . The implementation of domains are from Gymnasium [ Towers et al., 2024 ] and the DM-Control Suite [ Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020 ] . For ease of computation, we limit the horizon for each task to 200 steps. For policy, critic and simulator model, we use a feed forward neural network with two hidden layers of 256 nodes each and ReLU activations. The final layers are all linear with the following output • Policy: Mean and log standard deviation of the Gaussian from which the action is drawn. • Critic: Single output as the critic score. • Simulator model: Number of state dimensions outputs predicting the next state and an additional output predicting reward. We use an Adam optimizer with learning rate as 3 ​ e − 4 3e-4 for each model. The baseline only uses the task reward when optimizing the data collection policy while Algorithm 3 uses a uniform mixture of task reward and critic difference score, strategically seeking high error regions that are relevant for high reward policies. All experiments were performed on an internal cluster with 64 64 CPUs per worker and a H100 GPU. However, none of the neural networks and domains in our empirical evaluation require extensive compute and we believe that the results can be reproduced on a single consumer hardware machine with any modern GPU within as most 1 week of compute time.

sections.heading: Details on Narrow Passage Domain
sections.text: We define a continuous 2D domain where relevant model errors are concentrated in a small region that is rarely visited by uniform exploration, but strictly necessary for optimal policy performance: • State Space: 𝒮 = [ 0 , 1 ] 2 \mathscr{S}=[0,1]^{2} . Agent starts at ( 0.1 , 0.5 ) (0.1,0.5) . Goal region is x > 0.9 x>0.9 . • Action Space: 𝒜 = [ − 0.1 , 0.1 ] 2 \mathscr{A}=[-0.1,0.1]^{2} (velocity vector ( x ˙ , y ˙ ) (\dot{x},\dot{y}) ). • True Dynamics ( 𝖬 \mathsf{M} ): – Normal Region: s t + 1 = s t + a t + 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.01 ​ I ) s_{t+1}=s_{t}+a_{t}+\mathcal{N}(0,0.01I) . – The Wall: A barrier at x = 0.5 x=0.5 blocks all movement, except for a narrow passage at y ∈ [ 0.45 , 0.55 ] y\in[0.45,0.55] . – The Trap: Inside the narrow passage, there is a strong ”wind” pushing the agent down: y ˙ eff = y ˙ − 0.05 \dot{y}_{\text{eff}}=\dot{y}-0.05 . • Initial Simulator ( 𝖬 ^ 0 \widehat{\mathsf{M}}_{0} ): A naive linear model, s t + 1 = s t + a t s_{t+1}=s_{t}+a_{t} , trained on initial uniform random data. It likely learns free movement everywhere, missing the wall and the trap. While policies and models are stochastic (Gaussian) for experiments in control tasks, we here use a deterministic transition model. Then the 1-Wasserstein distance cleanly reduces to the expected distance between predicted and observed state. This simplification was an intended benefit of the experimental design. It allowed us to clearly visualize and validate that the critic was accurately learning the Error-MDP reward function without the added confounding variance of sampling from a stochastic learned model.

Abstract Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) agents typically learn world models by minimizing predictive loss. However, powerful RL optimizers inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies, leading to “simulator exploitation” and a reality gap where policies succeed in simulation but fail in the real world. We propose that the objective for learning simulators should be strategic robustness rather than predictive accuracy, and formulate this as a zero-sum minimax game between a model player and an adversarial policy player. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis: (1) an online learning guarantee showing the game is learnable with sublinear regret bounds; (2) a tractable critic-based simplification bounding the global policy-value gap by the local critic’s loss; and (3) an Error-MDP duality , proving that finding the worst-case policy is formally dual to a standard RL problem where the reward is the one-step critic error. This duality yields a provably convergent active data selection algorithm. Experiments on continuous control tasks demonstrate that our approach reduces prediction error in strategically important regions by 1.5 1.5 – 2.2 × 2.2\times and enables policies trained purely in simulation to match near-optimal real-world performance. 1 Introduction Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) represents a promising path toward agents with high sample efficiency, strong planning capabilities, and the ability to test policies in a safe, offline environment ( Sutton, 1990 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ) . In this paradigm, an agent first learns a simulator, or “world model” ( M ^ \widehat{M} ), from data collected in the real world ( M M ). Second, the agent trains its policy ( π \pi ) entirely within this learned simulator, using it as a fast and safe sandbox to find an optimal strategy. The critical flaw in this decoupled approach is the inevitable discrepancy between the learned model and the true environment. No matter how much data is collected or how large the model, the simulator is never a perfect copy of reality. This discrepancy leads to a well-known failure mode: the reinforcement learning algorithm, as a powerful optimizer, will inevitably discover and exploit the tiniest inaccuracies in the simulator’s physics or rules to achieve an artificially high score ( Chua et al., 2018 ) . This phenomenon, often called the reality gap or simulator exploitation , results in policies that are brilliant in simulation but fail catastrophically when deployed in the real world. The standard approach to simulator learning is to minimize a one-step predictive loss, such as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) or the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). This objective, however, is fundamentally misaligned with the agent’s downstream task. MLE optimizes for average predictive accuracy across all visited states, whereas the RL agent’s performance is determined by the worst-case, exploitable error along the specific trajectories it discovers. A model can have 99% predictive accuracy on average but fail on a single, crucial transition that an adversary can learn to visit repeatedly. Existing work has proposed several ways to mitigate this. One popular method is to learn an ensemble of models to quantify uncertainty ( Chua et al., 2018 ) and train a policy that is robust to this distribution. Another line of work, particularly in offline RL, introduces pessimism or conservatism, penalizing the agent for actions that deviate from the known data ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . A third category uses robust control formulations, but these often require a pre-defined and known ”uncertainty set” for the dynamics ( Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ; Wiesemann et al., 2013 ) , which is unavailable when the model is learned. More recently, adversarial methods have been explored. Some works introduce adversarial disturbances to the state ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) rather than the model itself. Others use Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to train the simulator, using a critic to enforce that one-step transitions are ”realistic” ( Volodin et al., 2023 ) . While promising, this still optimizes a local, one-step metric of realism. It fails to address the global, policy-level objective of strategic robustness . The critic does not ask, Is this transition plausible? ; it should ask, Can a policy exploit this transition to create an unrealistic, high-value trajectory? To bridge this gap from local plausibility to global strategic robustness, we argue for a new objective. We reframe simulator learning not as a prediction task, but as a two-player, zero-sum game between a Model Player (the simulator) and a Policy Player (the adversary). The Policy Player’s goal is to find the policy π \pi that reveals the largest discrepancy between the true value in the real world V π ​ ( M ) V_{\pi}(M) and the predicted value in the simulator V π ​ ( M ^ ) V_{\pi}(\widehat{M}) . The Model Player’s goal is to update its parameters to minimize this worst-case discrepancy. This leads to our central minimax objective: min M ^ ∈ ℳ ⁡ max π ∈ Π ​ | V π ​ ( M ) − V π ​ ( M ^ ) | \displaystyle\min_{\widehat{M}\in\mathcal{M}}\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\,\left\lvert V_{\pi}(M)-V_{\pi}(\widehat{M})\right\rvert (1) By solving this game, we produce a simulator that is not just accurate on average, but is specifically robust against being exploited by the very agent that will be trained within it. This formulation also provides a principled theoretical foundation for related proxy hacking problems, such as reward hacking in RLHF ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Christiano et al., 2017 ) and out-of-distribution exploitation in offline RL ( Levine et al., 2020 ) . Our contributions are as follows: • A Policy-Aware Minimax Objective: We formulate robust simulator learning as a minimax game and connect it to a practical online learning framework. We provide a regret bound (Theorem 3 ) showing that if the model player achieves sublinear regret, its average value-gap against the adversary also vanishes. • Tractable Critic-Based Guarantees: We show that the intractable policy-maximization max π \max_{\pi} in ( 1 ) can be relaxed to a tractable max D \max_{D} over a critic function D D . We provide finite-time guarantees (Lemma 4 ) that bound the true policy-value gap by the loss of this critic-based game, scaled by a coverage constant κ \kappa . • The Error-MDP Duality: We introduce our most significant theoretical novelty. We prove (Theorem 9 ) that the global problem of finding the worst-case policy π \pi is formally dual to a local RL problem: finding the optimal policy in an Error-MDP where the reward is precisely the one-step critic error. • Provably Stable Active Learning: We resolve the circular dependency between learning a model and collecting its counter-examples. We formalize active data selection as an iterative game and prove its convergence to a saddle point (Theorem 11 ). This guarantees that our critic-guided sampling mechanism is not merely heuristic, but a theoretically stable method for minimizing the coverage constant κ \kappa . • A General Framework for Proxy Hacking: We show this framework is a general solution for proxy hacking , with direct applications to solving reward hacking in RLHF and OOD-exploitation in Offline RL (Section 8 ). Related Work. Our approach intersects with several key areas. Uncertainty-aware MBRL relies on ensembles or pessimism to mitigate model error, whereas we actively seek and correct strategic flaws. Adversarial RL typically perturbs dynamics to robustify policies; in contrast, we perturb policies to robustify models. Finally, Value-Aware Model Learning weights errors by value gradients for a fixed policy, while our minimax formulation actively anticipates the worst-case policy shift. We provide an extended discussion in Appendix A . Paper Organization. The paper is organized as follows. Section 3 formalizes the landscape of simulator fidelity metrics and justifies our choice. Section 4 presents our first main result, an online-learning guarantee for the full minimax objective. Section 5 introduces our practical, critic-based simplification of the game and provides robust value-gap guarantees. Section 6 presents our novel theoretical results on active data selection, including the Error-MDP duality and convergence proofs. In Section 7 , we present an experimental validation of our theoretical results by examining a controlled 2D scenario. Section 8 discusses the broader applications of our framework to other proxy-hacking problems. Section 9 generalizes our framework to the joint learning of dynamics and rewards. 2 Setup and Notation We work with discounted Markov decision processes (MDP) ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , 𝖯 , r , γ ) (\mathscr{S},\mathscr{A},\mathsf{P},r,\gamma) with state space 𝒮 \mathscr{S} , action space 𝒜 \mathscr{A} , transition kernel 𝖯 ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) \mathsf{P}(\cdot\mid s,a) , reward function r ⁡ ( s , a ) ∈ [ 0 , R max ] r(s,a)\in[0,R_{\max}] , and discount factor γ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in(0,1) . Metrics and Desiderata Before formalizing our minimax objective, we must first establish what it means for a simulator to be good . In standard supervised learning, fidelity is measured by predictive accuracy on a fixed dataset. In reinforcement learning, however, fidelity is measured by the success of policies trained within the simulator when deployed in the real world. This distinction requires a careful choice of metric. Below we consider several notions of simulator fidelity, ranging from the strongest (trajectory-level) to the weakest (optimal-value only). 3.1 Trajectory or reward-free closeness Definition 1 . We say 𝖯 ^ \widehat{\mathsf{P}} is trajectory-close to 𝖯 \mathsf{P} (for horizon H H ) if some divergence between their finite-horizon trajectory distributions is small: D traj ( H ) ( 𝖯 , 𝖯 ^ ) = sup π ∈ Π D ( P 𝖯 π ( τ 0 : H − 1 ) , P 𝖯 ^ π ( τ 0 : H − 1 ) ) , D_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(H)}(\mathsf{P},\widehat{\mathsf{P}})=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}D\left(P_{\mathsf{P}}^{\pi}(\tau_{0:H-1}),P_{\widehat{\mathsf{P}}}^{\pi}(\tau_{0:H-1})\right), where D D is a divergence such as TV, KL, or Wasserstein. This is a reward-free criterion: if trajectory distributions match, then all reward functions measurable on trajectories, including state- or action-dependent ones, induce the same return distributions. It is extremely strong: matching trajectory distributions implies matching all marginals, including ( s , a ) (s,a) occupancies and one-step conditionals, but is infeasible for large or continuous state spaces. For discounted infinite-horizon problems one can instead consider the distribution over discounted trajectories. In practice, one truncates to large H H and weights by γ t \gamma^{t} .
